series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] mm/gup: convert follow_page_mask() to return a long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch changes the return type of the follow_page_mask() function from a struct page pointer to a long integer. The function can now return either 0, a negative error number, or 1 with the found page stored in a new pages[0] slot. This change is made to allow for future modifications that will carry a page count in the return value. The patch also updates several related functions and tests to accommodate this change without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] mm/gup: split follow_page_pte_commit() out of follow_page_pte()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the function follow_page_pte() into two separate functions: follow_page_pte_commit() and follow_page_pte(). The new function, follow_page_pte_commit(), handles the per-folio work of grabbing a reference to the page, making it accessible if necessary, marking it dirty or accessed if required, and flushing the cache. This change is intended to prepare for future modifications that will allow committing multiple pages at once. No functional changes are introduced by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] mm/gup: add gup_fill_pages() and use it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new helper function gup_fill_pages() to the Linux kernel's mm/gup.c file, which simplifies the process of filling pages in various follow functions (follow_huge_pud(), follow_huge_pmd(), and follow_page_pte_commit()). The new function replaces repeated code that stores the page found into pages[0] and flushes its caches. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] mm/gup: return a huge page's full count from follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the Linux kernel's mm/gup module to return a huge page's full count instead of requiring an additional try_grab_folio() call and subpage loop for large pages. The change involves adding an @end argument, having the huge paths report their count as the return value, and filling every subpage via gup_fill_pages(). This reduces lock contention and improves performance by minimizing the time spent holding a lock, especially for large folios.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the performance of __get_user_pages() by allowing it to walk multiple PTEs in a single call, rather than restarting the page table walk and re-taking the PTE lock for each page. This is particularly beneficial for large folios (mTHP) where the current approach results in significant overhead. The patch also introduces refcount batching, which reduces the number of times the kernel needs to grab references to pages. Measurements show a significant improvement in performance, with median get time reduced by up to 14.5x in certain scenarios.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves the performance of page table walks in Linux by batching contiguous pages together, reducing the number of lock acquisitions and walk restarts. The patches modify various functions to return a count of pages and an end pointer instead of individual struct page pointers, allowing for more efficient handling of large folios. Patch 5 is the only one that changes the number of page table walks or lock acquisitions, and it achieves significant performance improvements in benchmarks. The series also includes several minor code cleanups and refactoring steps to simplify the codebase.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH RFC] mm/gup: batch contiguous pages in follow_page_mask() and return them via a pages array

version_history.subject: [PATCH RFC] mm/gup: batch contiguous pages in follow_page_mask() and return them via a pages array

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way Linux handles page table walks by batching contiguous pages in the follow_page_mask() function and returning them via a pages array. This reduces the number of repeated page table walks, especially for PTE-mapped large folios, which can lead to significant performance improvements. The patch also simplifies the code by removing unnecessary loops and refactoring the logic to avoid restarting the walk at every folio boundary. Additionally, it fixes a silent correction in the old page_increm clamp, making it more robust and reliable.

review_comments.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer expressed frustration and concern about the patch's size and complexity, citing reviewer time constraints and requesting a more reasonable model for kernel development.
review_comments.raw_body:
OK it seems the message isn't really getting through...

You really have to spend at least some time filtering this LLM-generated
stuff.

Even as an RFC this isn't acceptable.

Reviewer time is hugely constrained and is still being done by the minority
of people.

Nobody's got time for walls of text and giant changes like this.

And at least use a reasonable model - sonnet isn't intended for kernel
development is it?

We may simply get to the point where people who have a habit of doing this
simply don't get to land series, so this is in your interests also.

Thanks, Lorenzo

Author acknowledged that the patch was too large and complex, split it into a series of 5 patches to simplify the changes and make them more manageable.

The author is addressing a concern about the quality of their patches, specifically mentioning that they produce 'unreadable LLM output' when left alone and need to follow rules to produce decent code. They acknowledge this issue and plan to add more rules to prevent it in the future.
review_comments.raw_body:
I spent a fair amount of time cleaning up the code
and comments. Arguably the new code is cleaner than
the old code was.

However, I do agree this patch is too big. That won't
happen again.

---

I had no idea how to split it up when I made it, 
but have found a few ways now.

I've split up the patch into a series of 5 now:
1) mm/gup: convert follow_page_mask() to return a long
2) mm/gup: split follow_page_pte_commit() out of follow_page_pte()
3) mm/gup: add gup_fill_pages() and use it
4) mm/gup: return a huge page's full count from follow_page_mask()
5) mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call

The changelogs naturally got shorter with things
split up this way.

---

Sonnet 5 seems to be about on par with Opus 4.7 from
last year. The difference is not that dramatic.

Also, I have found that while Opus tends to make fewer 
mistakes than Sonnet, they both produce unreadable LLM 
output when left alone.

In order for them to produce code that is at least a
good starting point for editing, they need to follow
rules.

Once you apply the rules, Opus and Sonnet do not
produce results that are all that different from
each other.

I just added a few new rules, so the tooling won't
even let me create too-large patches any more.


Whenever you see me, or somebody else, produce
something wrong, either with or without an LLM,
please yell at me, so I can add the proper rules
to kernel-style (creation side), or review-prompts 
(review side), so those things get caught 
automatically in the future, and not sent to the
list.

--

review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Lorenzo expressed concerns about the patch's readability and maintainability, specifically citing excessive use of walls of text, redundant code comments, and lack of refactoring to improve technical debt.

Reviewer Lorenzo (ARM) expressed disagreement with the patch, citing concerns about the quality of code generated by fable, a tool used in the submission process, and suggested using it as guidance only rather than implementing its suggestions directly.

Reviewer Lorenzo expressed strong disagreement with the patch, citing reviewer/submitter asymmetry and AI slop as major concerns, which he believes will lead to rejection of similar submissions in the future.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for doing a human pass but it LLM's habits really carried through
here. In general:

- No walls of text please - fewer words are better, clarity is king.

- Don't write the code in English as a comment/commit msg - redudant and
  distracting.

- Sensible patch separation obviously please.

- Write as elegant/reasonable code as possible. If the code you touch was
  some horrible mega-function, take the time to refactor it. Pay down
  technical debt.

These are all things LLMs are extremely bad at (even fable). So they need
to be done by a human.

---

Unfortunately based on your recent submissions I don't agree.

In general, even with fable, I've found that the code it generates is
nowhere near kernel quality.

I'd suggest using the generated code as guidance only and the LLM for
checking things rather than making things.

---

Well as you can tell I'm not afraid to - well I wouldn't say yell, more
civilised than that - protest :)

In general, again, the human layer is what's needed here not more rules
IMO.

Reviewer/submitter asymmetry was already a huge problem, AI slop makes it
critical and means people repeatedly submitting things that look like that
will get rejected out of hand.

Let's try to avoid that here :)

review_comments.summary:
The author is addressing a concern about the patch's adherence to kernel coding style rules and its readability, specifically regarding the use of comments and formatting. The author acknowledges that the code may not be perfect but explains that they are working on building a collection of kernel-style rules in a separate repository and plans to address these issues in future revisions.

sentiment_signals: acknowledges the value of AI-generated code

review_comments.raw_body:
LLMs can apply those rules, when expressed in a way
that they get interpreted unambiguously by the LLM.

I'm slowly building up a collection of such rules
in the kernel-style repository.

AI can write in any style you ask it to.

/*
 * Long in the Halls of Rq the weary wait,                   
 * till __schedule, herald of the turning years,             
 * calls forth the next to walk the road of fate             
 * as prev fades west.                
 */      

AI can also flag such issues, once it knows to
look for them.

---

The 80/20 rule comes into play here.

If AI produces junk, the person starting with
LLM-produced code can spend days cleaning it
up, without getting things in a reasonable state.

If the AI produces a better starting point, the 
remaining issues will stand out like a sore thumb, 
and it's much easier to find and fix them.

I agree there will always be a need for human
judgment, but that doesn't mean we should not
improve our tooling.


--
